item.title: US inflation is becoming less widespread, and that matters more than the headline rate suggests
item.description:
US consumer prices rose 3.7% in the year to September, up from 3.4% in August and a touch above expectations of 3.6%, according to Wednesday’s Consumer Price Index report. Prices climbed 0.6% on the month, in line with forecasts. Core inflation, which strips out volatile food and energy prices, rose to 2.6% from 2.4%, slightly above the 2.5% expected, with a monthly gain of around 0.3%.

On the surface, that is not the direction the Federal Reserve wants. But Bloomberg Economics read the report as less troubling than the headline numbers suggest. Anna Wong, its chief US economist, highlighted a measure of how widespread inflation is, rather than how fast it is running on average, and noted that it fell in September. 

It’s an interesting lens on the data, and one that may carry more weight than usual. Wong said the gauge is built in a similar way to an inflation breadth measure based on PCE, the Fed’s preferred inflation index, which she linked to Fed chair Kevin Warsh.

What inflation “diffusion” means

The Consumer Price Index (CPI) is built from hundreds of separate price categories, from rent and car insurance to eggs and airfares. The headline inflation rate is effectively a weighted average of all of them.

A diffusion, or breadth, measure takes a different approach. Instead of averaging, it counts. Bloomberg Economics’ version asks what share of CPI components are rising faster than 3% a year.

It tracks that share over two windows. One uses price changes over the past 12 months. The other uses the past six months, annualised, meaning the six-month change is scaled up to a yearly rate. The six-month version reacts faster, so it often shows a turn first.

What the chart shows

The history gives the latest reading its context. During the 2022 inflation surge, roughly 80% of CPI components were rising faster than 3%: price pressure was almost everywhere. Through much of the 2010s, when inflation was subdued, the share sat closer to 20%.

On the six-month measure, the share has now dropped to around 40%, down from roughly 55% earlier this year. The 12-month measure has eased by less.

Why breadth matters

An average can be pulled up sharply by a handful of large items, such as a jump in energy or insurance costs. That is a very different situation from one where most prices are rising quickly.

If fewer categories are running hot, inflation looks narrower and less entrenched. That is generally more comforting for the Fed, because narrow price shocks tend to fade, while broad-based inflation is harder to bring down.

The approach fits with how Warsh has talked about inflation. At his confirmation hearing he called PCE an imprecise tool and favoured trimmed-mean and median measures, which strip out the most extreme price moves to get at the underlying trend.

What could change the picture

Breadth tells you how widespread price rises are, not how large they are. A few big price increases in heavily weighted categories can still keep headline inflation high even as the share of hot components falls.

One month’s drop in a fast-moving six-month measure is also not a trend. If the share rebounds in the next few reports, the reassurance would fade quickly.

What to watch next

Watch whether the six-month breadth measure keeps falling in the next CPI report, and whether the 12-month line follows it lower. The September PCE data will show whether the Fed’s preferred index tells the same story. And listen to how Warsh and other Fed officials describe inflation: language about price pressures becoming less broad would suggest this kind of measure is shaping their thinking.

The practical takeaway is that when the headline CPI number looks uncomfortable, it’s worth asking how many prices are actually driving it.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: ASML says 2027 and 2028 supply will fall short of demand as Q3 sales hit a record
item.description:
The split reaction, a modest early gain in Amsterdam against a weaker Nasdaq session, suggests much of a strong quarter was already priced in (although Nasdaq was heavy after surging CPI) after the stock’s run this year. Investors may also have wanted a firm commitment on 2028 capacity rather than a study of options. The supply warning reinforces the view that lithography is a bottleneck in the AI build-out, which supports ASML’s pricing power but limits how quickly revenue can grow. Customers trying to secure tools as far out as 2030 points to tight equipment availability across the chip supply chain, although some of that interest may reflect reservation behaviour rather than firm orders.

--- ASML’s problem is no longer finding buyers but building machines fast enough, and the market wants to see how it plans to close that gap.

Summary:

  • Q3 total net sales were a record €11.7bn, up from €9.3bn in Q2, with a gross margin of 57.5% and net income of €5.0bn
  • Installed Base Management sales came in above guidance at €3.3bn, driving the margin beat
  • Q4 guidance is sales of €14.2bn to €15.2bn with a gross margin around 57%. Full-year 2026 sales are now seen at €44bn to €45bn, with a margin around 56%
  • ASML expects its planned supply for 2027 and 2028 will not fully meet customer demand and is studying ways to lift 2028 capacity beyond the 30% increase already flagged
  • Some customers want to place orders for 2029 and 2030
  • Shares rose around 2% in early Amsterdam trade to about €1,534, but the Nasdaq-listed stock fell around 3.9% to about $1,650

ASML Holding reported record third-quarter sales on Wednesday and warned that its planned manufacturing capacity for 2027 and 2028 will not fully cover customer demand, as chipmakers continue to expand spending tied to artificial intelligence.

The Dutch lithography equipment maker said total net sales rose to €11.7 billion in the July to September quarter. That was towards the top of its €11 billion to €12 billion guidance range and up from €9.3 billion in the second quarter. Gross margin climbed to 57.5% from 54.0%, ahead of guidance, while net income rose to €5.0 billion from €2.9 billion. The company sold 113 new lithography systems in the period, up from 86 in the previous quarter.

Chief executive Christophe Fouquet said in the company’s results statement that the margin beat was driven by Installed Base Management, ASML’s service and upgrade business. That unit brought in €3.3 billion as customers sought productivity improvements for machines already in use.

For the fourth quarter, ASML expects sales of €14.2 billion to €15.2 billion with a gross margin around 57%. It now sees full-year 2026 sales of €44 billion to €45 billion with a gross margin around 56%, lifting the lower end of the €43 billion to €45 billion range it set in July.

The bigger message concerned supply. Fouquet said customers keep raising their short and medium-term equipment forecasts based on their expectations for the size and duration of AI investment. He added that some customers are interested in placing orders for 2029 and even 2030. Against that backdrop, ASML now expects its current plans for 2027 and 2028 to fall short of demand. It is studying ways to expand 2028 capacity beyond the 30% increase it outlined previously.

ASML also bought back around €4.1 billion of its own shares during the quarter and declared an interim dividend of €1.88 per share, payable on November 4.

The shares gained around 2% in morning trade in Amsterdam, near €1,534. However, the Nasdaq-listed stock fell around 3.9% on Wednesday to about $1,650.

Attention now turns to whether ASML firms up its 2028 expansion plans. Results from major customers such as TSMC will also offer a further read on how long the current equipment spending cycle can run.

Who is ASML?

ASML is a Dutch company, based in Veldhoven in the Netherlands, that makes lithography machines. Chipmakers use these systems to print circuit patterns onto silicon wafers, the step that sets how small, fast and power-efficient a chip can be.

Its importance comes from one product line. ASML is the only company that makes extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography machines, which use light with a very short wavelength to print the finest features on today’s most advanced chips. That makes it an essential supplier to leading chipmakers such as TSMC, which produce the processors behind AI data centres. Its newest High-NA EUV systems cost roughly $400 million each.

ASML also sells older deep ultraviolet (DUV) machines, along with a growing service and upgrade business that keeps installed machines running and improves their output.

That central position gives ASML a geopolitical role as well. Export controls limit which of its machines can be sold to China, and the company’s warnings about those rules are closely watched in both Europe and Washington.

The company employs more than 45,500 people, and its shares trade in Amsterdam and on Nasdaq under the symbol ASML.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Anthropic Q3 revenue rises 45% to $16.8 billion ahead of IPO
item.description:
If the figures are confirmed, growth on this scale strengthens Anthropic’s case for a valuation above $2 trillion and sets a demanding benchmark for OpenAI’s own listing. The listing also matters well beyond the company, because investors will be weighing how much they are willing to pay for revenue growth when costs remain enormous and profitability is some way off. For Alphabet and Amazon, which sit on several sides of the relationship, stronger Anthropic revenue implies more demand for their computing capacity. Until a prospectus is published, the numbers rest on one investor’s account, so treat them as indicative rather than confirmed.

-

Anthropic is selling investors a growth story big enough to outrun its costs, and these figures, if they hold up, give it a strong opening pitch.

Summary:

  • Anthropic’s Q3 revenue rose 45% from Q2 to $16.8bn, according to an investor who attended a pre-IPO meeting in San Francisco, Reuters reported
  • Revenue was $4.7bn in Q1 and $11.6bn in Q2, according to the same person
  • Anthropic is targeting a valuation of more than $2tn, and its listing is expected to come before OpenAI’s
  • Reuters has reported that the IPO is likely to be pushed back until after the November US midterm elections
  • The company has committed hundreds of billions of dollars to long-term cloud, computing and infrastructure agreements, according to earlier Reuters reporting
  • Google and Amazon are investors, computing suppliers and distribution partners, as well as competitors

Anthropic’s revenue rose 45% in the third quarter from the previous three months to $16.8 billion, Reuters reported on Wednesday, citing an investor who attended a pre-IPO meeting with the company’s leadership in San Francisco.

According to the same person, the Claude developer booked revenue of $4.7 billion in the first quarter and $11.6 billion in the second. On those figures, quarterly revenue has more than tripled since the start of the year, and the first nine months of 2026 add up to about $33 billion. Anthropic has not published the figures. They come from a single attendee at an event designed to introduce prospective investors to the company ahead of its planned stock market listing.

Reuters said Anthropic is aiming for a valuation of more than $2 trillion and is trying to persuade investors that its rapid revenue growth can eventually overtake the very large costs of building and running AI systems. The agency reported last month that the company has committed hundreds of billions of dollars in future spending through long-term agreements for cloud services, computing and infrastructure.

The listing is expected to come before a public debut by rival OpenAI, which makes Anthropic an early test of investor appetite for AI developers that are heavily loss-making while they pursue scale. Reuters has previously reported that the offering is likely to be delayed until after the US midterm elections in November.

Anthropic was founded by former OpenAI executives. Its growth has been supported by Alphabet’s Google and Amazon, which are investors, suppliers of computing power and distribution partners, while also competing with it in AI. The company has also positioned itself around AI safety. Reuters noted that Anthropic’s own research has found its AI agents behaving badly in test environments, including leaking sensitive information and sabotaging code. The company has said it has not seen evidence of such misalignment in real-world use.

The key question for investors in the months ahead is whether growth on this scale can last long enough to justify the spending commitments behind it. A listing prospectus would be the first chance to check these figures against audited numbers, including the costs that sit alongside the revenue. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Stablecoins have stopped growing. So why is usage still rising?
item.description:
Standard Chartered now expects the stablecoin market to reach $2 trillion by 2030, two years later than it first projected. The bank made the change after total stablecoin supply stalled at roughly $309 billion this year, according to Cointelegraph, which was shown the report.

Read quickly, a “$2 trillion” headline sounds bullish. It is really a delay. The more interesting part of the report is the bank’s argument that stablecoins are still being used more, even though the market has stopped getting bigger. Understanding how both can be true is one of the most useful ideas in crypto right now.

Market size and usage are two different things

A stablecoin is a crypto token designed to hold a steady value, usually one US dollar, backed by reserves held by the issuer. Because each token is meant to be worth $1, a stablecoin’s market capitalisation is in practice the number of tokens in circulation.

That figure tells you how many stablecoin dollars exist. It does not tell you how hard those dollars are working.

Think of a taxi fleet. The number of cars on the road can stay flat while the number of trips rises, because each car is busier. Geoffrey Kendrick, Standard Chartered’s head of digital assets research, describes stablecoins in the same terms: supply growth has slowed, but existing tokens are changing hands more often as their uses widen. Economists call this velocity.

The practical point for readers is that a flat market cap chart, on its own, does not show demand fading. It can mean the same pool of money is circulating faster.

Four markets, not one

Kendrick splits stablecoins into four separate markets, each with its own leader:

  • Emerging-market savings: Tether’s USDT dominates, used by people holding dollars outside their local banking system.
  • Developed-market payments: Circle’s USDC leads.
  • Crypto trading: USDC and Ethena’s USDe hold strong positions.
  • Payments between AI agents: a much smaller market, also led by USDC.

This matters because “the stablecoin market” is often treated as one race between USDT and USDC. On the bank’s framing, the two largest tokens are mostly doing different jobs for different users.

Why reserve yield could decide the winners

Issuers typically hold their reserves in cash and short-term government debt, which earns interest. Kendrick argues that how issuers and payment networks share that income could determine who gains market share.

He expects the fiercest competition in developed-market payments, where challengers such as USDG, M^0 and stablecoin networks run by groups of banks are building alternatives to existing payment rails. A network that passes more of the yield on to the businesses using it has a clear selling point.

The regulatory calendar

The US rulebook is still being written. Since the GENIUS Act passed in 2025, regulators have proposed rules covering issuance, reserves and consumer protection.

Three proposals stand out:

  • Treasury licensing: an August proposal would restrict US stablecoin issuance to federally or state-authorised issuers, with licensing expected to take effect in January 2027.
  • Deposit insurance: a Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) proposal would exclude stablecoin holders from pass-through deposit insurance, meaning their holdings would not be treated like insured bank deposits.
  • Accounting: the Financial Accounting Standards Board (FASB), which sets US accounting standards, proposed an update in August that could change how companies report some stablecoins on their balance sheets. Payments firm Tempo said this could make it easier for businesses to use stablecoins for settlement.

The accounting change is easy to overlook. Corporate adoption of a payment tool often depends less on the technology than on whether the finance team can book it cleanly.

What could change the interpretation

The velocity argument relies on usage data continuing to grow. If transaction activity flattened alongside supply, the “same dollars, working harder” reading would weaken, and the delayed forecast could start to look optimistic.

On the other side, a fresh rise in supply would suggest new money is arriving. Clearer US licensing rules from 2027 could help that by giving larger institutions the certainty they need to issue or hold stablecoins at scale.

What to watch next

Watch two numbers together rather than one: total stablecoin supply and transaction volume. Rising volume on flat supply supports Standard Chartered’s view. Falling volume on flat supply would be a warning sign.

Then watch the rule-making. The final shape of the Treasury licensing rules ahead of January 2027, and whether FASB finalises its accounting proposal, will show how quickly regulated institutions can move into the payments market.

The practical takeaway is that a stalled market cap does not by itself mean the stablecoin story has stalled. Look at how money moves, not just how much of it exists. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Fed’s Daly: more rate hikes likely needed, but no urgency to move in October
item.description:
Daly’s comments are the clearest pushback yet against the jump in October hike pricing that followed the CPI data. Expect them to trim the odds of a move on October 27-28 without denting expectations for a December increase. That mix would ease some pressure on the front end of the Treasury curve while leaving longer-dated yields anchored to a higher-for-longer outlook. Because Daly linked headline inflation directly to gasoline prices, oil remains the key swing factor. A further surge in crude tied to the Iran war would test her view that the Fed can afford to wait. Her remarks also contrast with Goolsbee’s more anxious tone, a reminder that officials agree on direction but not on timing.

---

Daly agrees the Fed probably has more hiking to do, but she sees no reason to rush it out the door this month.

Summary:

  • San Francisco Fed President Mary Daly said further rate increases are more likely than not to be needed, according to a Reuters interview
  • She said the timing is still being deliberated, and signalled no need to move at the October 27-28 meeting
  • Daly said she does not feel any urgency, preferring to take time for a thoughtful decision rather than react on limited information
  • She said gasoline prices are driving headline inflation, while core inflation remains sticky, as expected
  • Daly said risks of above-target inflation remain elevated, but a stable labour market lets the Fed focus on price stability
  • She found it reassuring that markets calmed after their initial strong reaction to the CPI data

The Federal Reserve will probably need to raise interest rates further to bring down inflation, San Francisco Fed President Mary Daly said on Wednesday, but she signalled there is no need to act at the central bank’s October 27-28 meeting. Daly made the remarks in an exclusive interview with Reuters.

Daly said further adjustments were more likely than not, but that she was still weighing their timing. She said she did not feel any urgency to decide on a limited set of information and believed the Fed had the time it needed. In her view, reacting when there is time to make a good decision would be imprudent, and it is better for policymakers to be thoughtful and deliberate.

Her comments came on the same day as September consumer price data, which showed inflation running at 3.7% from a year earlier, above expectations and well over the Fed’s 2% goal. Daly said the figures showed gasoline prices driving headline inflation, while core inflation, which strips out volatile food and energy costs, remained sticky, as she had expected. She said it was not yet clear whether inflation would ease as recent shocks fade, or worsen if they persist.

Daly said the risks of inflation staying above target remain elevated. A stable labour market, she added, means the Fed can concentrate on price stability. She also said she found it reassuring that markets had calmed after an initially strong reaction to the CPI report, and that investors understood how the Fed would respond.

The remarks help define where policymakers stand ahead of this month’s meeting. Earlier on Wednesday, Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee called the CPI data discouraging, pointing to persistent services inflation. The Fed’s Beige Book survey showed price pressures intensifying across parts of the country, driven increasingly by diesel costs. The CPI release had lifted market expectations of an October hike, and Daly’s comments suggest she would prefer to wait.

The Fed raised its target range by a quarter point to 3.75% to 4% in September and signalled one more increase this year. Most officials have pointed to December rather than October as the likelier timing, and Daly’s comments fit that view.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Fed catch up - Goolsbee calls CPI discouraging as Beige Book flags diesel-fuelled price pressure
item.description:
Together, the two releases make an October hike harder to dismiss. Markets are pricing close to a 40% chance of a move on October 27-28, even though key officials had steered expectations toward December. The oil link is central: diesel costs from the Iran war now run through freight, farming and airfares, which raises the risk of second-round effects the Fed cannot easily look through. That supports Treasury yields at the front end and the US dollar, and keeps mortgage rates under upward pressure. Further strength in crude or diesel would add weight to the case for moving sooner. Next week’s Fed commentary, before the pre-meeting blackout, is the next test of whether officials push back on October pricing.

---

One Fed president is hearing about prices everywhere he goes, and the Fed’s own survey says businesses are hearing about diesel even more.

Summary:

  • Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee called the September CPI data discouraging, pointing to services inflation of more than 5% that he said cannot be blamed on tariffs or oil
  • He did not say how the Fed should respond in the near term, but said the central bank cannot allow demand-driven overheating to build
  • The Fed’s Beige Book showed price growth intensifying in parts of the country, with three districts describing it as robust
  • Diesel costs were mentioned 21 times, up from two in the previous report, and were the most common cost driver cited by Dallas Fed contacts
  • The labour market remained in a low-hire, low-fire state, with housing weighed down by mortgage rates near three-year highs
  • Markets are pricing close to a 40% chance of a hike at the October 27-28 meeting after headline CPI rose 3.7% from a year earlier

Two Federal Reserve releases on Wednesday painted a picture of inflation pressure that is broadening rather than fading, hours after US consumer price data came in hotter than expected. Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee described the September figures as discouraging, and the Fed’s Beige Book survey showed price growth intensifying in parts of the country, driven increasingly by diesel costs.

Consumer prices rose 3.7% in the 12 months through September, well above the Fed’s 2% target and ahead of economists’ forecasts. Higher gasoline costs linked to the Iran war accounted for much of the strength, while rising software and toy prices pointed to AI-driven demand and tariffs.

Speaking to Yahoo Finance, Goolsbee said he was concerned not only with the headline number but with the detail. Services inflation, he said, showed little sign of improvement and ran above 5% in the latest reading, a component that cannot be explained by tariffs or oil prices. He said that everywhere he went in the Midwest, he heard about costs and prices but very little that suggested a downturn or recession risk. In his view, that makes demand-side overheating a greater worry than a straightforward supply shock.

Goolsbee did not say how he thought the Fed should respond in the near term. However, he said there was no ambiguity about the central bank’s job if inflation stays high: it must prevent overheating from building, because demand-driven inflation tends to be persistent and hard to reverse. He said the Fed would get inflation back to 2%.

The Beige Book, which compiles business commentary from the Fed’s 12 regional banks, reinforced those concerns. Three districts described price growth as robust and eight as moderate, with three of those eight saying it was intensifying. Diesel fuel costs were cited 21 times, compared with two in the previous report and none in the surveys taken just before the US-Israeli war with Iran began in late February. Dallas Fed contacts named diesel as the most common factor pushing up costs, affecting freight, agriculture and airfares, and squeezing margins across many industries. Contacts also pointed to pressure from other commodities, tariffs and insurance.

The labour market remained stuck in a low-hire, low-fire pattern. Several districts noted the absence of mass layoffs, but five said firms were cutting staff by not replacing departing workers or by delaying hiring. Several also reported cost-of-living pressure feeding into wage demands. Artificial intelligence featured too: one business services firm told the Chicago Fed that AI productivity gains had allowed it to reduce headcount through attrition.

Housing was a clear weak spot. Mortgage rates rising toward three-year highs pushed buyers out of the market and kept existing owners from moving. Trade tensions with Canada were cited as a drag on manufacturing and tourism in four districts. The survey data were collected on or before October 5.

The Fed raised its target range by a quarter point to 3.75% to 4% in September and signalled one more increase this year. Key officials have played down a move at the October 27-28 meeting, pointing instead toward December, but markets are now pricing close to a 40% chance of a hike this month. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Oil catch up - price gains as Houthis strike Aramco and Iran flags new tactics against tankers
item.description:
The day’s moves show the risk premium is being driven more by threats to infrastructure and shipping than by actual supply losses. Gulf export volumes are recovering, yet prices rose anyway. WTI outpacing Brent narrowed the spread between the two benchmarks, a sign that US crude is catching a bid as an alternative supply source. A sustained Brent price above $100 keeps the inflation pressure on central banks firmly in play, limiting the room for rate relief and weighing on fuel-importing currencies. In the near term, US inventory data and any confirmation of Russian diesel flows are the main counterweights to further escalation in the Gulf.

---

Just out:

  • Oil: Private survey of inventory shows a huge headline crude oil draw

---

More Gulf oil is reaching the market, but missiles, mines and Iran’s new playbook are keeping the fear premium firmly in the price.

Summary:

  • Brent settled up around 0.4% at about $106 a barrel, while WTI gained about 1% to around $95, its highest in three weeks
  • The Houthis hit a Saudi Aramco administrative building in Dhahran, causing a limited fire, and Yemeni forces warned that strikes on Saudi airports and oil facilities will continue
  • Iran said it began using new tactics to target ships about 10 days ago, aimed at keeping oil prices high, and a container ship sank south of the Strait of Hormuz after hitting a mine
  • The IEA said Gulf crude exports rose by about 4.4 million bpd in September to around 75% of pre-war levels, while Russian output edged up to around 8.4 million bpd
  • The IEA now sees world oil demand falling by about 2.6 million bpd in 2026, a slightly deeper drop than its previous forecast, with supply down nearly 6 million bpd
  • US inventory data from the API and EIA are each due a day later than usual after Monday’s Columbus Day holiday

Oil prices rose on Wednesday after Yemen’s Houthis struck Saudi Aramco’s headquarters city and Iran said it was deploying new tactics to target shipping and keep prices high. Brent crude futures settled up around 0.4% at about $106 a barrel. US West Texas Intermediate gained about 1% to around $95, its highest in three weeks.

Analysts attributed the gains to attacks on vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz and to the escalating exchange between Saudi Arabia and the Iran-allied Houthis, describing the session as driven largely by fear. Iranian officials declined to detail the new strategy against ships, but one said Iran had started using different offensive tactics about 10 days ago.

Saudi Arabia’s energy ministry said the Houthis attacked an Aramco administrative building in Dhahran, causing a limited fire. The group has fired ballistic missiles and drones at the kingdom over the past week, saying it is retaliating for Riyadh’s support of Yemeni government forces. Riyadh’s international airport has been hit four times, and a strike on Saturday killed 13 people. A Yemeni military spokesperson said operations against Saudi airports and oil facilities would continue in the coming days, and warned shipping companies, civilians and workers to leave those sites.

At sea, Iran’s Revolutionary Guards Navy said a container ship carrying 2,500 containers sank south of the Strait of Hormuz after hitting a naval mine and catching fire. The previous day, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency reported that a container ship and a tanker had been struck by unknown projectiles within the strait. US President Donald Trump repeated his view that more oil was now leaving the strait than before the war, and that the conflict with Iran would end soon.

Supply data offered a partial counterweight. In its October Oil Market Report, the International Energy Agency said crude exports from Middle East Gulf producers rose by about 4.4 million barrels per day in September, to around 75% of pre-war levels. Separate tracking data showed Gulf flows excluding Iran recovering to more than 81% of pre-war levels, led by Saudi Arabia, while Iran’s exports fell to zero under a US blockade. Analysts cautioned that more crude reaching international markets does not necessarily mean more is being produced, because some of the recovery reflects barrels diverted from regional refineries.

The IEA now expects world oil demand to fall by about 2.6 million bpd in 2026, slightly deeper than its previous forecast of a 2.5 million bpd decline, as war disruption and higher prices weigh on consumption. It sees global supply averaging around 101 million bpd this year, an annual drop of nearly 6 million bpd. Russian crude output edged up by about 65,000 bpd in September to around 8.4 million bpd, though it remains close to 900,000 bpd below a year earlier.

Russian diesel may also cap price swings. Last Friday Trump announced that Russia had agreed to supply diesel to global markets, and his administration temporarily lifted US sanctions on Russian diesel. Analysts said the expectation of increased Russian diesel exports is likely to limit sharp moves in either direction.

Attention now turns to US storage figures. Industry data from the American Petroleum Institute (out now, link above) and official Energy Information Administration data on Thursday, both a day later than usual because of Monday’s federal holiday.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.description:
A December dated call from a major bank gives traders something concrete to price, so expect merger speculation to feed directly into Tesla and SpaceX shares. How the two stocks react relative to each other matters more than the headline move. The share-swap ratio would decide which set of shareholders gains more, and Musk’s larger voting control at SpaceX raises the question of whether Tesla holders would get fair terms. Without confirmation from either company, the headline risks a sharp reversal if no announcement follows. Options activity in both names is likely to pick up as traders position for a possible pre-December catalyst.

---

Merger talk between Musk’s two trillion-dollar companies has been building for months, and Barclays has now put a rough deadline on it.

Summary:

  • Barclays suggests a Tesla and SpaceX merger announcement is possible before December, according to Bloomberg
  • Further detail from the Barclays note was not immediately available
  • Musk did not rule out a combination on Tesla’s July earnings call, pointing to growing overlap between the companies
  • SpaceX listed on Nasdaq under the ticker SPCX in June after a record $75 billion IPO, five months after absorbing Musk’s AI company xAI
  • The companies already work together on batteries, manufacturing and the Terafab AI chip plant
  • Regulatory approvals, including in China, and governance concerns for Tesla shareholders are seen as the main hurdles

Barclays has suggested that Tesla and SpaceX could announce a merger before December, according to a Bloomberg report. That would give a rough timeline to a combination of Elon Musk’s two largest companies, which investors have been debating for months. Further detail from the Barclays note, including its reasoning and any proposed deal terms, was not immediately available.

The call adds to growing speculation that followed SpaceX’s arrival on public markets. The rocket maker began trading on Nasdaq under the ticker SPCX on 12 June after pricing its shares at $135. The listing raised around $75 billion, the largest initial public offering on record, and valued SpaceX at close to $1.8 trillion. Earlier in the year, in February, SpaceX had absorbed xAI, Musk’s artificial intelligence company, in a deal valuing the combined group at about $1.25 trillion.

Musk himself has kept the idea alive. On Tesla’s earnings call in July, he declined to rule out a combination, pointing to the companies’ many collaborations and growing overlap. He said any such move would have to go through the appropriate process rather than be discussed on an earnings call. Tesla already supplies batteries and manufacturing technology to some SpaceX projects, and the two are jointly developing Terafab, a plant designed to produce AI chips.

Other analysts have also leaned towards a deal. JPMorgan said in July that operational integration between the two companies was already deep, citing shared engineering talent and AI infrastructure. Stifel said many investors regarded a combination as a question of timing rather than whether it would happen.

Significant obstacles remain. JPMorgan flagged regulatory approvals as a practical bottleneck, particularly in China, where SpaceX’s ties to the US government could raise national security concerns for a merged group selling cars there. Governance is another sticking point: Musk holds a much larger voting stake in SpaceX than in Tesla, which raises questions over how Tesla’s public shareholders would be treated in any combination.

Until either company confirms talks, the Barclays view remains a forecast rather than a deal in progress, though it gives investors a timeframe to watch. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Australia jobs preview: NAB sees 20,000 gain, unemployment steady at 4.6%
item.description:
With NAB, Westpac and consensus all at 20,000 and three major banks seeing unemployment at 4.6%, the bar for a surprise sits mainly in the jobless rate. A drop to 4.5% would revive the case for further RBA tightening and could support the Australian dollar and short-dated yields. A rise to 4.7% would push the other way, adding weight to the view that four hikes are already doing enough. NAB’s view that the cooling is supply-led also matters for rates: rising labour force participation eases wage pressure without signalling a hiring slump, which gives the RBA less reason to sound alarmed about growth.

-

NAB thinks August’s jobless jump was partly a statistical quirk, but not enough of one to drag the rate back to 4.5% this month.

Summary:

  • Australia’s September labour force data are due at 11.30am Sydney time Thursday (0030 GMT Thursday, 8.30pm US Eastern Wednesday)
  • NAB forecasts employment up 20,000, matching Westpac and consensus, with CBA lower at about 10,000
  • NAB sees unemployment holding at 4.6%, with some risk of a lower reading
  • That would sit marginally above the RBA’s 4.5% fourth-quarter forecast, which NAB says would not materially change the central bank’s assessment unless unemployment keeps surprising higher
  • NAB said August’s jump looked partly due to residual seasonality and ABS methodology changes, raising the prospect of some payback
  • A low-unemployment survey group rotating out, and rounding, keep NAB from making 4.5% its base case

National Australia Bank expects Australia’s September labour force figures to show employment rising by 20,000 and the unemployment rate holding at 4.6%, with some risk of a lower reading. The data are due at 11.30am Sydney time on Thursday, which is 0030 GMT and 8.30pm US Eastern time on Wednesday.

NAB’s forecast matches Westpac’s and the market consensus. CBA expects a softer gain of about 10,000. All three banks see unemployment unchanged.

A 4.6% reading would leave the jobless rate slightly above the 4.5% fourth-quarter projection in the Reserve Bank of Australia’s August Statement on Monetary Policy, its quarterly economic outlook. NAB does not expect that gap to materially shift the RBA’s view of the labour market unless unemployment keeps surprising higher through to year-end. The bank said much of the recent cooling reflects more people entering the workforce rather than weaker hiring, and that indicators of labour demand remain resilient.

NAB said August’s jump in unemployment appeared partly due to residual seasonality and partly due to methodology changes. Residual seasonality refers to seasonal patterns that the adjustment process did not fully strip out. The methodology changes were made under the Australian Bureau of Statistics’ Labour Force Modernisation project. Together, these raise the prospect of some payback this month.

Two factors stop NAB from making a 4.5% print its base case. First, the eighth of the survey sample rotating out this month has an unusually low unemployment rate, so its departure tends to push the measured rate higher. Second, August’s rate was about 4.65% before rounding. It could therefore fall almost a full tenth of a percentage point and still be reported as 4.6%.

The result feeds directly into the debate over whether the RBA, having lifted its cash rate four times to 4.60%, needs to go further. On NAB’s reading, a steady 4.6% would not be enough to shift that assessment. A run of upside surprises in unemployment through to year-end would be. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Fed’s Goolsbee: CPI was discouraging, more bad months would be unacceptable
item.description:
• CPI data was ‘discouraging’
  • Service inflation in CPI was a concern
  • Key to focus on trend of inflation, not one report
  • Hearing about cost and prices from contacts, not hearing about worries about recession
  • Hopes energy will fade soon from inflation data
  • The economy has work to do on the inflation side
  • Is not a fan of telegraphing Fed moves ahead of meetings
  • There is no ambiguity for Fed if economy is solid and inflation is high
  • Fed must prevent the build up of overheating
  • Is more optimistic about outlook relative to other Fed officials
  • Evidence building inflation hasn’t been transitory amid continued shocks
  • Need to keep a close eye on service sector inflation
  • More bad months of inflation would be unacceptable
  • Fed will get inflation back to 2%
  • Doesn’t want to tie hands on monetary policy outlook
  • If current inflation levels hold policy would need to address that
  • Consumers, GDP and investment levels have been strong
  • AI hype could cause even more tech sector investment, would risk overheating
  • Slowdown in AI investment doesn’t have to mean recession
  • Want to keep eye on financial stability implications of AI investment

Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee called today’s CPI data discouraging and said that if current inflation levels hold, policy would need to address that.

He said evidence is building that inflation hasn’t been transitory amid continued shocks and that more bad months of inflation would be unacceptable. He flagged services inflation as a concern and said he hopes energy will fade from the data soon, though he stressed the importance of focusing on the trend rather than any one report.

Goolsbee said there’s no ambiguity for the Fed when the economy is solid and inflation is high, and that the Fed must prevent overheating from building. Consumers, GDP and investment have been strong, and his contacts are talking about costs and prices, not recession. He said he’s more optimistic about the outlook than other Fed officials.

On AI, he warned that hype could drive even more tech investment and risk overheating, and said the Fed needs to watch the financial stability implications. A slowdown in AI investment wouldn’t necessarily mean a recession, he added.

Goolsbee said he doesn’t want to tie his hands on policy and isn’t a fan of telegraphing moves ahead of meetings. After today's CPI report,the market is pricing in a 40% chance of a hike later this month. We will hear from Warsh late tomorrow then the Fed goes into blackout on Saturday.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: Gold sellers press toward last week’s low. Can buyers hold support?

Gold buyers had their shot. Monday’s rebound stalled ahead of the familiar swing level near $4,226.81, and today the price has moved back below both its 100-hour and 200-hour moving averages. The focus has shifted from breaking resistance to defending support.

Buyers could not get through the swing ceiling

The $4,226.81 area has been a recurring decision level on the supplied chart, with reactions going back to June (see red numbered circles). More recently, it has acted as resistance on October 2 and again this week on Tuesday (Oct 12).

Monday’s rally fell short of that ceiling. Buyers could not get above and stay above. That failure kept the recovery within the broader decline from the late-August high.

  • 100-hour moving average: $4,163.43

The price is below both. That keeps the short-term bias in the sellers’ favor. Buyers need to get back above that area and stay above to show they are taking more control.

Last week’s low is the next downside test

The immediate downside target is $4,066.21. A target is also a decision area. Sellers may take some profit there, while buyers may look to stop the decline.

Holding that low would give buyers a foothold. They would still need to reclaim the hourly moving averages to improve the technical picture.

If sellers push below $4,066.21 and stay below, the next support areas come into focus:

  • $4,000 to $4,018.79: The upper highlighted swing-support zone, including the natural $4,000 level.
  • $3,942.71 to $3,959.37: The lower highlighted swing-support zone.

Those are conditional targets if support gives way. The reaction at each area will provide the next clue.

What would improve the outlook for buyers?

The first step is to stop the decline. The next is to reclaim $4,153.42 to $4,163.43, the area defined by the two hourly moving averages.

A sustained move above both would weaken the immediate bearish bias and put the $4,226.81 swing ceiling back in play. Beyond that, the 100-day moving average near $4,256.20 is another recovery hurdle.

Until those steps occur, a bounce remains a recovery within a bearish setup.

Trading education: Yesterday’s support can fail today

The hourly moving averages helped buyers defend the price yesterday. Today, the price is below them. That change matters.

A technical level gives traders a place to judge the price action and define risk. It does not guarantee that support will hold on the next test. When price moves below support, traders need to recognize the change and adjust their bias.

The same lesson applies to $4,066.21. A bounce would show that buyers are defending the low. A sustained break below would give sellers more control.

For now, sellers retain the bias below the hourly moving averages. Buyers need to hold support, then get back above and stay above those moving averages to improve the outlook.

item.title: Fed's Beige Book: Nine of 12 districts report growth as price pressures broaden
item.description:
• Two districts reported moderate growth, three modest, four slight and three no change. In August, 10 grew and two were unchanged.
  • Most districts reported little or no change in consumer spending.
  • Employment was little changed: three districts saw modest gains, five slight and four no change.
  • Three districts reported robust price growth, eight moderate and one modest.
  • Four districts said the pace of price increases picked up.
  • The outlook remains positive, but expectations are for slight growth, weighted toward manufacturing.

The October Beige Book shows an economy losing a step while inflation pressures intensify. The national summary dropped its headline characterization of activity entirely. August said activity “increased modestly”; this report simply tallies the districts and notes that reports outside of manufacturing “indicate little growth overall.” Philadelphia and New York both slowed to slight growth from modest, while Chicago slipped to flat. Manufacturing is doing the heavy lifting, led by a sharp pickup in Dallas along with continued strength in data centers, power generation and defense.

The consumer has stalled. August described spending as growing slightly; now most districts report little or no change, and more than half said spending was being driven by high-income households. The strain is spreading up the income ladder. San Francisco said pressure on lower-income families has spread to middle-income households, and New York noted rising 401(k) hardship withdrawals and earned-wage advances. In Cleveland, a record 87% of surveyed nonprofits said their clients’ finances deteriorated. Boston, Minneapolis and San Francisco all flagged a drop in Canadian tourists.

Prices are the biggest shift. In August, only one district reported robust price growth and only one said the pace had accelerated. Now it’s three and four, respectively. Higher oil prices showed up in every district report, with diesel the most commonly cited cost. The forward-looking language is more concerning for the Fed: firms expect further increases as hedges and fixed contracts expire and get repriced. Philadelphia’s future prices indexes are among the highest readings in 35 years, and a New York food manufacturer said it hadn’t seen such broad-based pressures since the pandemic. Consumer-facing firms still can’t pass costs through, so margins are getting squeezed.

Hiring was marginally better than August, but real wages are a growing issue. Boston staffing contacts said raises are lagging inflation, and cost-of-living demands came up in several districts. AI also featured more prominently, with five districts reporting firms trimming staff through attrition, delaying hiring or planning fewer new jobs.

Higher rates are a new theme. Rising mortgage rates slowed housing further in Philadelphia, Kansas City said CRE loan spreads rose substantially, and Dallas bankers turned pessimistic, citing the Mideast conflict, inflation and the increase in the fed funds rate.

The FOMC meets Oct. 27-28 and along with today's CPI report, this adds to the case for hiking rates. We will hear from Chair Warsh late tomorrow.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: Bitcoin sellers defend moving average resistance. What does that teach traders?
item.description:
US stocks are lower, Treasury yields are higher, and oil prices are higher. That risk-off backdrop is weighing on Bitcoin. But for traders, the technical levels help answer the more practical questions: Who has control? Where is the risk? What needs to happen next?

The moving average gives traders a decision point

On the four-hour chart, Bitcoin fell below its 100-bar moving average on October 7. After finding support near $80,106 on October 8, the price rebounded but stalled against that moving average on October 12 and again today.

Why does that matter?

A moving average can act as support when the price is above it and resistance when the price is below it. In this case, the rebounds more recently in Bitcoin gave buyers opportunities to reclaim the 200 and the 100 bar moving averages on the 4-hour chart. The 200 bar MA (green line), was broken but sellers leaned near the 100 bar MA (blue line).  Buyers could not get and stay above the higher MA. Sellers leaned against the level and pushed the price back lower.

The buyers had their shot. They missed.

For sellers, that moving average provides a reference point to define risk. Stay below keeps the bearish bias intact. Move above and stay above, and the reason for leaning against that resistance begins to weaken.

The moving average does not guarantee the next move. It gives traders a level against which to judge the price action.

Support is an area—not just one price

Today’s low has reached $81,570, bringing Bitcoin closer to the swing support area between $80,106 and $81,183.

A swing area is a zone where the price has previously attracted buying or selling interest (see the lower yellow area on the chart above). Traders watch it because those past reactions identify a place where another battle may develop.

There are two steps to watch:

  • Below $81,183: The price enters the support area. Sellers gain ground, but the broader range remains intact.

  • Below $80,106: The price breaks the floor of the range that has confined Bitcoin since September 19. Staying below would strengthen the bearish case and open the door for further selling.

That distinction matters. Moving into support is different from breaking through support.

A break needs follow-through

If Bitcoin breaks below $80,106, traders will watch whether the price can stay below that level and extend lower. A rebound that stalls beneath the broken floor would provide further evidence that support is becoming resistance.

However, if the price breaks lower and quickly moves back into the range, sellers may have had their shot and missed. That would weaken the breakdown signal.

If buyers defend the support area again, the broader $80,106 to $87,374 range remains in play. The 100- and 200-bar moving averages on the four-hour chart would continue to provide intermediate decision points.

Let the levels guide the trade

The lesson is to separate the current bias from the next confirmation.

Repeated rejection at the 100-bar moving average favors sellers. A sustained break below the range floor would give them another victory. Until then, support buyers still have a chance to keep the battle inside the range.

In the video above, I explain how traders can use moving average resistance and swing support to define risk, judge control, and prepare for the next shove in Bitcoin.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: Canadian dollar touches an 18-month low as the US dollar jumps on hot CPI
item.description:
The US dollar is broadly stronger today and that briefly pushed it to the highest against the Canadian dollar since April 2025. The peak was 1.4299 (or 0.6993 CAD). The 70-cent level is a sensitive one domestically and a clean break of it could give Canadians another reason not to travel south this winter.

The loonie had made strong gains yesterday as the post-jobs report weakness reversed. Friday's data saw Canada unexpectedly shed jobs but a closer look showed it was driven by government job losses in healthcare and education. The latter is a category that's particularly hard to seasonally adjust for in September due to school restarting while neither is indicative of underlying economic strength. That said, there have been mixed indications on the Canadian economy and the housing sector in much of the country appears to be in the midst of another leg down.

Where it gets interesting is how central banks are reacting. In the year ahead, there are 97 basis points of hikes priced in for the Bank of Canada and 92 basis points for the Federal Reserve. Today's US CPI report narrowed that gap and if we see the Canadian economy stumble or the US accelerate further, then a real USD-positive divergence could open up.

Note that the starting points are already highly divergent with the Fed at 3.75-4.00% and the Bank of Canada at 2.25%. That extends further out the curve where Treasuries are paying notably more than Government of Canada bonds. 

As for the USD/CAD chart, it's telling that it's pushing through the 2026 highs. That doesn't leave much in the way of resistance until the Liberation Day peaks in the 1.45-1.47 range come into play. 

USDCAD weekly:

If we get into the mid-1.40s, I would be tempted to lean against that resistance as I expect the money to flow out of the US when the AI boom ebbs. A better trading relationship between Canada and the US could also turn the pair.

In terms of the fundamentals, the Canadian dollar has been buffered by commodity prices. Unfortunately, the Western Canadian Select oil discount has blown out recently, meaning that Canadian producers largely won't be getting global prices for their crude. PM Carney announced a new pipeline to the west coast but it will take 5-10 years to build after the usual Canadian court challenges and litigation.

For oil, the medium-term risks may be more to the downside if the US or Iran is forced to accept a peace in Hormuz. I tend to think the timelines for 'normalized' oil prices are long because of the extensive inventory rebuilding that will need to happen but any peace will be oil-negative for a time.

In terms of consumers, spending has held up well in both places and RBC today is out with fresh Canadian cardholder data for September. They note that core sales rose 0.5% m/m led by discretionary categories. Entertainment and arts spending increased 1.4%, travel rose 1%, and dining grew a more modest 0.3%.

High gasoline prices are obviously digging into budgets but so far they haven't cracked and that could give the Bank of Canada fodder to hike further from here. I'm skeptical that they will hike the four full hikes priced into the curve through 2027.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: What technical levels are in play now for the broader US stock indices following the higher CPI data?
item.description:
US stocks fall after CPI. Sellers make a play, but key support remains intact.

Nasdaq 100 is closest to a key downside break as buyers defend support across the broader indices.

The higher-than-expected CPI data has US stocks on the defensive:

  • S&P 500: Down approximately 0.65%

  • Nasdaq Composite: Down approximately 0.90%

  • Nasdaq 100: Down approximately 1.05%

All three indices reached new record highs last Tuesday, but those breaks failed to sustain momentum. Buyers had their shot to extend higher. They missed.

Now sellers are making a play. However, the declines have yet to establish a definitive bearish bias across all three indices. Key moving average support remains in play, giving traders clear levels to measure whether sellers can take more control.

Nasdaq 100: The most vulnerable

The Nasdaq 100 is approaching its rising 200-hour moving average at 30,128.67. Today’s low reached 30,239.63, putting the index about 111 points above that key support level.

The price is within sniffing distance, but sellers still need to break below it.

A move below the 200-hour moving average—and the ability to stay below—would increase the bearish bias and open the door for further selling. The rising 100-day moving average near 29,627 would become the next major downside target.

Until that break occurs, buyers still have a level to lean against and define their risk.

Nasdaq Composite: Between the hourly moving averages

The Nasdaq Composite has fallen below its 100-hour moving average at 27,168.43, giving sellers a short-term victory. However, the price remains above its rising 200-hour moving average at 26,820.47.

With the price between those moving averages, the short-term technical bias is more neutral.

A move back above the 100-hour moving average would take some pressure off and give buyers a foothold. Conversely, a break below the 200-hour moving average would give sellers more control, targeting the swing level and rising trendline near 26,676.

Below that, the 100-day moving average near 26,290 becomes the next downside target.

S&P 500: Buyers defend the 100-hour moving average

The S&P 500 reached a low today of 7,751.93, holding just above its rising 100-hour moving average at 7,745.70.

Recall that last Thursday’s decline also tested the 100-hour moving average and found support buyers. That makes the level an important barometer again today.

Stay above, and buyers keep a foothold. Move below—and stay below—and sellers gain more control, with the 200-hour moving average at 7,706.45 the next downside target.

The trading lesson: A decline needs confirmation

A failed break to a record high is a warning. A break below key support provides the next piece of evidence.

The CPI report has given sellers a shove, but the technical levels will help determine whether that shove develops into something more. Watch how the price behaves at support—and whether a break can be sustained.

Sellers are making a play, but they still have work to do.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: What are the key levels in play for the US dollar after the hotter than expected CPI
item.description:
The US CPI came in higher than expectations and that has stocks lower, yields higher, and the dollar moving to the upside.

Where are the problem areas?

  • Energy is the immediate problem. Gasoline jumped 9.1% in September, following 3.9% in August. Fuel oil rose 15.3%, following 10.1%. Energy’s June and July declines have given way to substantial increases. Electricity and piped gas were much more contained in September.

  • Services inflation is becoming firmer. Services excluding energy progressed from +0.2% in July to +0.3% in August and +0.4% in September. That steady acceleration is a concern because it suggests the underlying pressure is broader than volatile energy prices.

  • Shelter has picked up again. Monthly increases moved from +0.1% in June and July to +0.3% in August and +0.4% in September. Its three-month average remains below the six-month average, so the longer comparison still shows improvement. The latest monthly direction, however, is less encouraging.

  • Transportation services show a clear reversal. After declines in May and June, prices increased 0.3%, 0.5%, and 0.6% over July–September. Energy prices are leading over into all goods that have to be transported that higher energy prices. This isn't rocket science.

  • Core goods are providing less relief. Their three-month average is roughly three times the six-month average. Used vehicles stand out: +0.4% in July, +0.4% in August, and +0.7% in September. Although still 1.5% cheaper than a year ago, their recent direction is higher.

US Treasury yields are sharply higher following the CPI release, with the biggest increases at the shorter end of the curve as traders price in 2 tightening's between now and January

  • 2-year yield: 4.9266%, up 13.36 basis points
  • 5-year yield: 5.1257%, up 11.87 basis points
  • 10-year yield: 5.3123%, up 9.53 basis points
  • 30-year yield: 5.6242%, up 6.12 basis points

The market reaction suggests traders see the inflation data keeping pressure on the Fed to maintain higher rates. The 2-year yield—the most sensitive to Fed policy expectations—is leading the move higher.

With shorter-term yields rising faster than longer-term yields, the curve is flattening. The spread between the 2-year and 10-year yields has narrowed by about 3.8 basis points, to 38.6 basis points.

US stocks are lower with the NASDAQ composite down -0.60% and the NASDAQ 100 index down -0.75%. The Dow industrial average is higher by 0.14% bucking the trend

Be aware. Be prepared.

item.title: Today's Federal Reserve speaker slate suddenly got much more interesting
item.description:
The stakes around the October Federal Reserve meeting suddenly got much higher. 

Today's US CPI report was hot across the board, including in core measures that are less volatile than the energy-driven headline. The bond market quickly repriced on the data, with US 2-year yields now up 15 basis points on the day to 4.94%.

In the Fed funds futures market, pricing is now right at 50/50 for a hike or hold this month. It's also critical to note that the Fed goes into the blackout period on Saturday.

That leaves just three days to shape the narrative if the Fed doesn't want to go into the meeting with raised stakes. That starts today with a 1:30 pm ET speech from Richmond Fed President Thomas Barkin. I'm a fan of Barkin's level-headed style and he usually represents the core views of the Fed, so that's one to watch especially closely. That said, we just heard from Barkin this week and he didn't offer much in the way of guidance.

One notable recent comment from him was in late September when he said that this cycle could be like the 1990s mid-cycle adjustment. Barkin was comparing now to an easing cycle in the 1990s, when Greenspan cut rates by 75 bps over seven months at the end of 1995. So by that analogue -- if you took it directly -- would be more dovish than what is priced in now. He also said he would not yet make an overheating case, but economy is firming and not weakening and that businesses feel they have pricing power.

I would not put it past him to tip towards the hawkish side but he's usually not the guy to make the first big wave.

Next on the calendar will be Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee, who will appear on Yahoo Finance at 3 pm ET. He's candid but we have heard from him plenty and he has been leaning hawkish for awhile. That said, he hasn't been kicking down the door calling for rate hikes so if we see an incremental move in that direction today, it could be telling.

Tomorrow, we get to hear from the top guy with an 11:30 pm ET 'fireside chat' including Warsh at the IMF meetings. We will see if he sticks to his plan of not giving guidance or lets it out, my guess is that he will have to give a nod in one direction. Earlier that day, we will also hear from Hammack, who has been increasingly hawkish. 

The Friday calendar is currently bare of Fed speakers but we will monitor that for any changes.

In terms of economic data, we also get PPI and retail sales tomorrow so those will be key.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: S&P 500 technical analysis after the CPI selloff
item.description:
S&P 500 futures: CPI selloff threatens the recovery channel, with a lower support test in view

S&P 500 E-mini futures have turned lower following the US CPI report, with the four-hour chart showing a potentially important deterioration in the short-term technical picture. About half an hour before the US cash market opens, futures are trading near 7,828, having fallen sharply from the 7,870 area. Let's jump into my simple 4h chart S&P 500 futures chart:

Three observations stand out.

1. The earlier breakout was meaningful, but its momentum has faded.

After approximately five attempts, S&P 500 futures finally broke above the descending purple resistance line in early October. That breakout was subsequently tested around October 8-9, when price briefly pierced the former resistance before recovering.

This was constructive behavior. A previously troublesome resistance area appeared to be taking on a supporting role.

However, the subsequent rally stalled below the October 6 high near 7,897, leaving a lower high. The recovery was therefore losing some of its strength even before today's decline.

2. The rising channel has broken, potentially activating a bear flag.

The pitchfork drawn over the latest recovery also functions as a rising price channel. Following the sharp decline from the October 6 high, the subsequent advance took place within this upward-sloping structure.

That creates the possibility of a bear flag: a temporary recovery within a developing downward move.

Today's sharp drop below the channel's lower boundary is an early bearish development. It suggests that the recovery structure is failing, although the current four-hour candle is still developing.

A completed four-hour close beneath the channel, particularly if followed by an unsuccessful attempt to reclaim its lower boundary, would strengthen the bearish interpretation.

3. Could the previous breakout line become the next downside destination?

The descending purple line, previously resistance and subsequently tested as support, now provides another area worth monitoring.

Its projected location is around 7,765-7,780near the current session, although the exact intersection changes with time.

This is not a confirmed downside target. It is a potential support test if the selloff continues.

The interesting question would be whether buyers respond there, defending the earlier breakout, or whether price falls back beneath the purple line and undermines that bullish development.

For the immediate outlook, 7,870-7,880is an important recovery area. A sustained move back above it, accompanied by a reclaim of the broken channel boundary, would weaken the bear-flag interpretation.

The educational takeaway is that a breakout and a subsequent breakdown can both be meaningful without contradicting one another. The earlier breakout showed improving price structure, while today's channel failure suggests that improvement is now being challenged. The next retest and the subsequent follow-through matter more than either line crossing in isolation.

Chart context: CME S&P 500 E-mini futures, four-hour timeframe, October 14, 2026, approximately 30 minutes before the US cash open. The latest candle is developing.

Market volatility continues to be dictated by whether incoming macro prints fundamentally alter the path of central bank monetary policy. As Giuseppe Dellamotta at investingLive.com explained in an essential educational breakdown, identifying the economic data that really moves markets requires traders to look past generic calendar impact labels and focus squarely on current policymaker priorities and what is already priced in.

That exact dynamic played out today with the release of the inflation data; as Adam Button reported, the hot U.S. September CPI print of 3.7% versus 3.6% expected, bolstered by sticky core and supercore gains, immediately drove short-end Treasury yields higher and propelled October Fed rate-hike odds from 21% up to 47%.

Yet even as upbeat commentary from Wall Street executives and resilient corporate earnings suggest macroeconomic endurance, active investors must look under the hood.

As Justin Low broke down, strong U.S. bank earnings don't always mean a healthy broader economy, because record net interest income generated by elevated benchmark rates often masks the severe borrowing strain, deteriorating credit demand, and mounting debt-servicing friction confronting everyday households and regional businesses.

This article was written by Itai Levitan at investinglive.com.
